name: Soviet anti-Zionism
summary: Soviet anti-Zionism was the official Marxist-Leninist campaign, strongest from 1967 to the mid-1980s, that treated Zionism as the ideology of the wealthy Jewish bourgeoisie allied with imperialism, as chauvinist, racist and anti-communist, and as an enemy of national liberation. It denied that the Jews of the world form one nation, favoured assimilation where they live, accepted Israel's existence while demanding withdrawal from occupied land, and defended Soviet Jews as part of the Soviet people. Scholars describe much of its propaganda as antisemitic, which Soviet officials denied.
scope: The Soviet state's anti-Zionist doctrine and campaigns from Lenin's rejection of the Bund and Zionism through Yuri Ivanov's Caution: Zionism! (1969-70), the Kichko literature on Judaism and Zionism, and the 1983 manifesto and Anti-Zionist Committee. Only positions the doctrine states about Zionism, Jews, Israel, nation, race and colonialism are answered; general Soviet-state or Marxist-Leninist features (economy, party rule, state structure) are left null. It excludes Stalin's pro-Israel policy of 1944-48 and Western anti-Zionism after the USSR.

notes:
Themes searched: world, society, culture and globalism (nation, Israel, colonialism, race, assimilation, refugees, withdrawal, anti-communism), plus economy, government, liberty, ecology, technology and means. The sources record no position of their own there, and the general Marxist-Leninist or Soviet-state features of the old audit (planning, public ownership, party rule, welfare, unions) are null here because they are not stated about Zionism. Scholars (s2) report that much campaign writing, including authors the state published, drew on the Protocols; the official line denied this. The Great Soviet Encyclopedia entry on Zionism and the UN debate texts were not retrievable, so they are not cited. The Anti-Zionist Committee manifesto is known here through a news report.

claude-sonnet-5-5+GPT-6.1-Sol notes: Independent re-audit from sources; earlier answers were not consulted. Searched the downloaded primary texts by theme, including economy (property, credit, wages), government (elections, courts, parliament), world (war, territorial withdrawal, refugees, UN, nuclear weapons), liberty (emigration and repression), culture (Hebrew, assimilation, identity), society, ecology and technology. Economic descriptions of alleged Zionist finance are not a domestic economic programme; the sources provide no distinct environmental or technology policy. Statements about all diasporas, all indigenous peoples or private self-defence are not answered as stated positions from one regional case. The original source’s allegations are reported as its claims; critics’ assessments are used to document campaign practice and context, not substituted for the doctrine’s own positions. Final evidence check leaves nearby-case extrapolations unknown where no stated general principle establishes the broader claim.
